reading.body:
CH4's published IT capacity is 36 MW. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 36 MW of IT load is roughly 900 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a common colocation average, the same power supports roughly 3,600 racks. The assumption you make about rack density changes the answer by a factor of four, so the published megawatt figure is the only hard number to reason from. No published specifications for cooling headroom, raised-floor area, or power redundancy tier appear on the source page, so no further architectural claims can be derived.

NTT holds no certifications listed in the data provided, so no certification-based qualification statement can be made. CH4 ranks second among the six Illinois facilities on this site that publish a megawatt figure, accounting for roughly 15 percent of the 236 MW of published IT capacity across that group. Illinois has 44 facilities mapped in OpenStreetMap, but only 6 publish a capacity figure, meaning the 236 MW total almost certainly understates the state's real installed base by a wide margin.

For a reader sizing AI infrastructure, 36 MW is a meaningful block of power in a state where the median published facility figure is far smaller, but it is not hyperscale territory by current AI campus standards, where single campuses are now announced at hundreds of megawatts. Whether CH4 supports dense GPU workloads depends on cooling and power delivery specifications that are not published. The campus sits in the Chicago metro, which the state context does not rank against other metros, so no regional grid or interconnection advantage can be asserted from the data given.
